what: Terex makes heavy equipment. Its products are aerial work platforms and telehandlers that lift people and materials on construction sites, cranes, and the crushing and screening machinery used in quarries and recycling. It recently added a large environmental and waste equipment business.
customers: Equipment rental companies, which buy a large share of the output, plus construction contractors, quarry operators, utilities and waste collection companies.
money: Boom lifts, scissor lifts and telehandlers, mostly sold to rental fleets.
Crushers, screens and washing equipment for quarries, mining and recycling.
Refuse collection vehicles and waste handling equipment, the recently acquired business.
moat: Heavy equipment is bought on brand, dealer support and resale value: a rental company cares what the machine is worth in five years, which favours established names with dealer networks that can service them. The environmental business is less cyclical than construction equipment, because refuse trucks are replaced on a municipal schedule rather than with the building cycle.
risks: Equipment demand is cyclical and dominated by rental companies, which can stop ordering abruptly when utilisation falls.
Debt is about $2.7B against $772.0M of cash, raised largely for the environmental acquisition, which has to earn its cost.
The shares trade at about 24.1 times earnings, which is a full price for a cyclical equipment maker.
Net income of $198.0M on $7.5B of revenue is a thin margin, typical of heavy equipment and leaving little room for error.
Tariffs and steel costs feed directly into the cost of building machines.
opportunities: Revenue has grown from $3.9B in 2021 to $5.4B in 2025, with trailing revenue of about $7.5B including the acquisition.
The environmental business is genuinely less cyclical: refuse trucks get replaced on municipal schedules regardless of construction activity.
Free cash flow of $419.0M exceeds net income of $198.0M, which indicates the cash generation is better than the earnings line.
Infrastructure spending supports demand for aerial platforms, crushers and screens.
Thirteen analysts average a $74.35 target, about 40% above the current price.
watch: Rental company order patterns and fleet utilisation. Rental firms buy a large share of the aerial equipment and they order based on how busy their existing fleet is, so their utilisation leads Terex’s revenue by a couple of quarters.
view: The thing to understand about Terex is who actually buys its products. A large share of the aerial work platforms goes to equipment rental companies, not to contractors, and rental companies order on a simple rule: when their existing fleet is busy they buy more, and when it is not they stop immediately. That makes Terex’s revenue a derivative of rental fleet utilisation rather than of construction activity directly, and it means the orders turn before anything shows up in construction data. If you follow one external number for this company, follow that.

The acquisition of the environmental business is more interesting than the usual bolt-on and deserves to be judged on its own terms. Refuse collection vehicles are replaced on municipal replacement schedules — a city budgets for new trucks on a cycle and buys them more or less regardless of whether anyone is building houses. Bolting a non-cyclical business onto a deeply cyclical one is a sensible answer to the central problem of being Terex, and if it works, the whole company deserves a higher multiple than heavy equipment normally gets.

Whether it works is the open question, and $2.7 billion of debt is what was spent to find out. Acquisitions of this size in cyclical industrials have a mixed record, and the integration happens while the core business faces soft construction demand — which is the hardest moment to do it. Free cash flow of $419 million against $198 million of net income is encouraging, and suggests the cash economics are better than the margin implies.

At 24.1 times earnings on a thin 2.6% net margin, the market is already paying for the diversification to work and for construction to recover. That is a lot of assumptions stacked together for a cyclical. The thirteen analysts at $74.35 are underwriting both. I would want evidence that the environmental segment is earning its cost of capital and that rental utilisation has bottomed before paying this, and I would treat the current multiple as the reason to be patient rather than the reason to act.
bull: The environmental business proves genuinely non-cyclical and earns its cost, rental fleet utilisation turns, and a diversified Terex re-rates above the heavy equipment multiple.
bear: Rental companies stop ordering into a construction slowdown while $2.7 billion of acquisition debt sits on a 2.6% margin business, and 24 times earnings meets a cyclical trough.
